lines: Thursday, 14 May 2026
Housekeeping
PRESIDENT:  Good morning.  This is
the first day of the evidentiary hearing in
DIAC arbitration no. 240079 between China State
Construction Engineering Corporation
(Middle East) LLC and Dubai Integrated Economic
Zones Authority.
First of all, can I welcome everybody to
London.  For some it's a shorter journey than
for others.  But I'd like to again record the
thanks of the tribunal to the Ruler for
facilitating this hearing, and again repeat our
concerns and hopes: concerns for what's going
on, and our hopes for a resolution of what's
going on in the Middle East as soon as
possible.  It obviously weighs on everybody,
and particularly people in this room.
From the transcriber, a reminder which, in
the usual way of things, we'll probably have to
do again and again: microphones on when
speaking, off when not speaking, please.
The list of attendees: we've received
a combined list, that's very helpful.  And
I'm assuming, Ms Cheng, that I will get
a similar list of attendees each day for the
following day.
MS CHENG:  We can certainly arrange that.
PRESIDENT:  Yes.  Having received that,
nevertheless, just as a matter of courtesy so
people will know, would you like to introduce
those who are beside you and in the room?
MS CHENG:  Sir, I think that's a very good
idea, but it's one with which -- for certain
people, I've met these people for the first
time today, so if I may defer to Ms Wertman to
act as my junior for that.
My name is Serena Cheng KC, I appear for
the claimant.  On hopefully every other day of
this hearing, I'm going to appear in
conjunction with Dr Nicholas Maciolek.
He passes you his apologies: he has a prior
commitment in the TCC today.
MS WERTMAN:  Thank you.  I'm Roberta
Wertman with Eversheds Sutherland, for the
claimant.  Next to me is Daniel Xu of Hourani
& Partners, for the claimant.  Next to him is
Isabelle Ferguson of Eversheds Sutherland, for
the claimant.  And then we have -- I'm going to
have to ask for help with the pronunciation
again.  Shall I pass to you, Daniel?  Okay.  Oh
dear.
PRESIDENT:  I don't think the microphone
is going to stretch all the way down to the end
of the table.
MR XU:  Good morning, tribunal.
So we have, from the claimant, China State
Construction, Mr Mahadev Viswanathan, and
Mr Lee See Hee from China State.  And the rest
of the team at the back: the lady in white is
Ms Sonia Thomas, and then Mr George Yong to her
left, and then Mr Low Boon Chin and
Mr Selvanayakam Mariappan.
PRESIDENT:  Now let's see if Mr Rigney can
identify everybody on his part.
MR RIGNEY:  (Off mic) I was going to see
if I could take an easier way out.  I'm very
helpfully told that everybody would be
delighted to introduce themselves!
Yes, you did predict that you would need
to tell people during the course of the
hearing; perhaps you hadn't anticipated quite
so early.
I am Andrew Rigney KC.  I am leading
counsel on behalf of the respondent in this
arbitration.
MR MAXWELL:  Good morning.  I'm
Patrick Maxwell, I'm junior counsel for DIEZA
in this arbitration.
MR YAHIA:  Good morning, everyone.  Good
morning, Mr Chairman and members of the
tribunal.
My name is Naief Yahia and I'm the lead
counsel from Al Tamimi & Company, representing
the respondent.  I have also my colleague Malak
Nesriddine, who is also a part of the Al Tamimi
team.  Justin Zhang -- I'm not sure if I say it
right -- is also part of the respondent's team,
and I also have Shuaib Mubeen and Lara, who
didn't arrive yet; she will arrive in a minute.
Behind, we have Tom Kapapa, Mr Tom Kapapa,
who is our delay expert.  We also have Mr Lee,
who is the GC of DIEZA.  We have Iman Salem --
sorry, surname is always a trouble to me, to be
honest -- Iman Salem, who is also part of
DIEZA's team; Anisha, also from the Legal
Affairs Department; and Ms Zahara Rose Khawaja
is also part of the Legal Affairs Department.
And --
MR MAXWELL:  Do you want me to do that
one?
MR YAHIA:  Yes.
MR MACIOLEK:  And Alastair Bloor, who is
a pupil in chambers.
PRESIDENT:  Good.  Thank you very much.
MR YAHIA:  Thank you.
PRESIDENT:  As we can see, these
proceedings are being transcribed.  The
dinosaur in this room, that's me, and a trainee
dinosaur, Mr Thomas, would like to have
hard-copy transcripts, please.  As far as
I'm concerned, they can follow at the end of
hearing, but I think Mr Thomas would probably
like them as they go along.
MR THOMAS:  Yes, I would, please.  And
that would be -- speaking for myself, anyway --
four pages to a page.
PRESIDENT:  Right.  For me, please, A5,
one page to a page format.
On the question of documentation,
I'm going to raise this for each party to think
about.  We think it could be very useful to
have particularly a separate hard-copy bundle
of the documents referred to.  Obviously there
may be limits, because some may be enormous
schedules and that sort of thing.  But we all
know that in these sort of arbitrations, there
is a vast amount of documentation in the
electronic file, and even in an eight-day
hearing, a limited amount is referred to.  But
I think that should be a matter of discussion
between the parties as to the logistics of
that, and timing and when you want to do it and
that sort of thing.
While on the subject of documents, can
I raise this.  It's my experience with the sort
of electronic documents system we have here
that the moment you get into hand-to-hand
fighting with the quantum experts, for example,
and up comes the schedule, which is 400 columns
wide, it can take quite a while for that to
download.
It's extremely helpful if you could speak
to the document manager ahead of each day or
each session and give early warning of
particularly Excel spreadsheets that you're
going to be bringing up, so anything that looks
as though it may take time to download, because
we can find ourselves spending quite a lot of
time on downloading.  So if you could think
about that.
These points are not necessarily in
logical order; they're just as they came into
my head, really.  That shows how confused my
head is!
There are some new cases which were
referred to in an email.  Mr Rigney, do you
have any -- were they coming from your side?
MR RIGNEY:  Yes.
PRESIDENT:  They were, sorry.
Ms Cheng, do you have any problem with the
additional couple of cases that Mr Rigney says
he may refer to?
MS CHENG:  No.
PRESIDENT:  Good.  Thank you.
We've had a list of issues from both
parties; thank you very much.  Is there any
prospect of those lists of issues being merged
and coming into one list?  It does look as
though there has been quite a lot of progress,
because in the ones last summer, one list was
very short and one list was very long; whereas
now, simply in terms of numbers of pages,
they're getting closer together.  And we are
now in the final stages of this arbitration.
Mr Cheng, what's your view about being
able to amalgamate these?
MS CHENG:  We can certainly amalgamate
them.  I suspect that there's some mileage in
attempting further to agree them at some point.
PRESIDENT:  Right.  It may be the parties
will think that should be an exercised carried
out between the close of this hearing and
service of closing submissions.
MR RIGNEY:  Sir, that was going to be my
suggestion.  I think it's probably incumbent on
the parties to do as much as they can on the
list of issues in order to assist you.  So
perhaps if we can endeavour to do that exercise
as soon as practicable after the close of the
hearing but in advance of the submissions,
at least then, if we can agree that, there's
a framework to which everybody can be working.
PRESIDENT:  Thank you.
The protocol, very helpful.  Have the
parties agreed a timekeeper on each side?  If
not, could that be done, just to make sure that
if there are any disputes, they are brought to
my attention.
One particular point on the protocol:
it provides for witnesses to give their
evidence on oath.  I assume that there is no
witness who finds that problematic.
At the moment I haven't made any
arrangements for any of the holy books to be
present.  Has anybody arranged for the
necessary holy books?
MS CHENG:  Yes, the agreement between
the parties is oath or affirmation, in case
someone has a problem with the oath.  We have
the holy books.
PRESIDENT:  Okay.  All right.  Good.
Powers of attorney.  We received the power
of attorney covering Mr Rigney and Mr Maxwell.
I raised a question in an email as to whether
or not there are any outstanding issues on
powers of attorney.  I've received no answer,
so I assume that everybody is content?
MS CHENG:  Correct.
PRESIDENT:  Mr Rigney?  Or it's down the
line, yes.  Good.
I raised the question a little while ago
about authorities, legal authorities, and in
particular translations.  Have the parties had
an opportunity to discuss whether there are any
issues as to translation of any of
the authorities?
MS CHENG:  Both parties have discovered
that the quotes that have been set out in each
of our submissions do not necessarily match
with the translation that's been provided,
which may have been what the tribunal very
helpfully was highlighting.
We have produced those to the other side,
the other side have produced theirs to us, as
part of our errata.  We're still considering
those.  I don't expect there to be any problem
at all.  But that is the reason for the delay
to your agreed list of authorities, which we
will have with you within the next two days.
PRESIDENT:  That sounds very helpful.
Good.
I did mention a possible bundle of
authorities; it seems that there's some
discussion.  That question of hard copies of
authorities can wait until perhaps closing
submissions, when we see which ones are really
in play at that stage and which are not.
MS CHENG:  I see.
PRESIDENT:  Obviously we will need to
discuss at some later stage timing of closing
submissions.
The assumption is that nobody will be
seeking any further hearing for closing, but if
I give notice now that we'd like to know by the
end of the hearing to see if anybody is
pressing for oral hearings.  I think, given the
difficulties, we probably will try to do that
remotely.  But anyway, hopefully we can avoid
it in any event.
Finally, as far as the tribunal is
concerned -- apart from anything I'm told from
either side I've forgotten -- times today.
I was assuming that we would break for
lunch at about 1 o'clock.  Now, we've got
45 minutes for lunch, and I think that's what
we agreed, and we've got to fit in a coffee
break halfway through.  So it may be that we
should look in terms of having the lunch break
at perhaps 1.15, so that the opening
submissions hopefully will be completed within
that time, being roughly an hour and a half
each, give or take a minute or two.
Is that acceptable?
MS CHENG:  Yes.
PRESIDENT:  Right.
Ms Cheng, any other housekeeping issues
from your side?
MS CHENG:  If I may, sir, just three
points: things about things that you've
received, things about things that you haven't
received, and things about things that
you might receive.
In terms of things you've not received,
I just want to put on the record that the
claimant is very grateful to the tribunal and
to the respondent for allowing the tribunal to
consider the whole of our opening, even if it
came in in two tranches, and we apologise again
for the inconvenience that that will have
caused.
The tribunal will note that our opening
sets out in great detail everything we wish to
say post-memorials about those issues that are
to be decided on paper, but the respondent's
does not.  Now, I make no criticism of them for
that, and I'm not making an application at this
stage.  But I do want to put on the agenda for
the tribunal and for my learned friend to think
about whether there ought to be provision for
some sort of responsive closing on those
on-paper items from the claimant.
I say that because if it is not done that
way, you won't have the benefit of any response
from us to the post-memorial position adopted
by the respondent, including in relation to
the post-memorial position adopted by the
respondent on those counterclaims where we are
the defendant.  As I say, it's not something
that needs to be decided today and it's not
something that needs to hold up these
proceedings; I just put it on the agenda.
Things that you have not received: sir,
you've very helpfully dealt with already
the bundle of authorities.
Things that you may soon receive: those
instructing me have contacted those instructing
my learned friend this morning because we would
like to seek leave to adduce a single item of
project correspondence into the bundle.
I don't think my learned friend has had
a chance to look at that yet, and I don't make
the application now, but I will make it when
he's had time to think about it.
In a similar vein, you will have noticed
that in the errata you received from the
respondent last night there are, I think two
items of project correspondence.  And this is
my fault: I haven't looked at them yet.  But
when I do, I will come back to my learned
friend as to whether we object to those; and
again, hopefully something that can be dealt
with by agreement.
PRESIDENT:  Okay, noted.
Mr Rigney, obviously have a think and come
back to the tribunal about any further
submissions on the matters.  We don't want it
in writing; I don't think we need to resolve
that now.  But any other points of
housekeeping?
MR RIGNEY:  Not for the respondent.
PRESIDENT:  Right.  Thank you very much.
Right.  Then on that basis, Ms Cheng,
the floor is yours.
MS CHENG:  Thank you.  Thank you, sirs.
Opening statement by MS CHENG
MS CHENG:  You have our written opening
and I'm more than happy to take any questions
on points that the tribunal may have on points
that aren't clear or where I've simply not made
any sense, but I don't propose to repeat it.
What I want to do is instead respond to the
points arising out of my learned friend's
written opening.
Again, there's a difference, a disparity,
in what we've done: we've served something that
runs to something like 300 pages and my learned
friend has perhaps the Ozempic version of that.
And it may be, in those circumstances, that
he goes slightly longer in oral opening, which
I think he has indicated he may do, and
I suspect I will go shorter than the time set
out in the timetable for my response.
If that is to be the case, may I suggest
that I use what remains of the time left in the
timetable, if any, to reply to the development
that my learned friend wants to put to you
orally.  Okay.
I would quite like to start where the
respondent wants you to start.  Is it
Mr Manliguez on the EPE?  In any event, EPE,
could I please have {B17-4}, and this should be
the introduction of the respondent's opening
submissions.
PRESIDENT:  I'll just stop you for
a moment.
I think I must be on some sort of loop
where if I don't touch the transcript, it goes
into resting mode.  And also I tried what
I thought was the password and it didn't seem
to work.  (Pause)
Ms Cheng, sorry to interrupt you, but
I've now got, I think, the transcript.
MS CHENG:  Thank you.  I think that's
probably quite helpful for me, given the speed
and the pace at which I speak.
As I say, I want to start where the
respondent wants you to start with their case.
Their introduction introduces the respondent's
case on liability by reference to two things:
the cooperation agreement and notices.  If
we take those in turn.
The cooperation agreement is the
claimant's engagement of a company called
6th Bureau.  6th Bureau is a sister company of
China State: they are both owned and controlled
by the same China State behemoth parent.
The involvement of 6B is said by the
respondent to be the cause of the contractor
delay and incompetence which it says besets
this project and is at the heart of this
dispute.  What is said is that that contract
was prohibited by the clauses of the contract
that prohibit an assignment or the formation of
a joint venture, and it's said to be contrary
to the Government Contracts Law 2020.
The respondent's theory of the case on
delay is not born out by the evidence.  As to
delay, the delay experts agree that
milestones C and D were delayed by the
electrical works and the finishing works.
As to the electrical works, these were
conducted by China State's MEP internal
division; 6th Bureau had nothing to do with
them.
The finishing works were designed by DAR's
sub-consultants.  They were supplied and, in
the case of artwork, they were installed by the
respondent's nominated sub-suppliers and
subcontractors.  There's no evidence that
the involvement of 6th Bureau caused or
contributed to any delay that's material to
these proceedings, and we will say that that
delay was instead caused by the late change of
the designs provided by DAR to the respondent's
instructions and to do with their timing.
The respondent's theory of the case on
defect is also not borne out by its own
counterclaim.  Notwithstanding the allegations
of 6B incompetence, half of the items included
in the defects counterclaim are MEP works,
which were again excluded from the cooperation
agreement.
So even if our works are as defective as
they're alleged to be -- which they are not --
that is not to do with 6B.  The counterclaim
is, we will say, instead the product of, first,
the disconnection between the respondent's
expectations and the claimant's contractual
obligations as agreed at the outset of this
project, coupled with the claimant's decision
in or around 2022 to stop servicing all of the
respondent's demands, this being, at this
stage, around two years after the defects
notification period had ended.
Further, and foundationally, the
claimant's theory of the case on liability is
in whole unsupported by the contract and
unsupported by the law.  The provisions of the
cooperation agreement that are complained of
are at {B17-14}, please.
MR THOMAS:  Forgive me, I have now lost
the transcript.  (Pause)
PRESIDENT:  Yes, Ms Cheng.  I apologise.
MS CHENG:  No problem at all.
So you see on screen, at paragraphs 33.2
and 33.3 and onwards, the provisions of the
cooperation agreement.  (Pause)
You see on the screen there the provisions
of the cooperation agreement with which the
respondent takes issue.  And at 33.2, that
agreement provides, on the second line, that
6th Bureau is:
"'... to shoulder all responsibilities and
obligations imposed by the contract on
[China State] on a back to back basis' ..."
"6th Bureau agreed to 'perform the Works
on a back to back basis and in accordance with
the same terms [and] conditions [et cetera] as
[are] defined in the Contract, together with
the project team assigned by [China State] to
the extent ... set out in the [Cooperation]
Agreement' ..."
EPE, could I also please have {D63-5}.
And it's clause 4.5 on the bottom, where we see
also that 6th Bureau -- and we know that's
6th Bureau because of the S in
the abbreviation:
"... agrees to perform, confirm, and abide
by all instructions, directions, and decisions
issued to [it] by CME."
Who is China State Middle East.
So the claimant thereby subcontracted part
of the burden of its contract with the
respondent to 6th Bureau.  It's common ground
that we agreed to pay 6th Bureau for
6th Bureau's work.  It's not alleged that
6th Bureau had any right of direct recourse to
the respondent for payment.
The terms relied on by the respondent as
being breached by the agreement the terms of
which I've just taken you to are at {D39-9},
please, and it's clause 1.7:
"Neither Party shall assign the whole or
any part of the Contract or any benefit or
interest in or under the Contract.  However,
either ...
"(a) may assign the whole or any part with
the prior agreement ... at the sole discretion
of [the] other Party ..."
I'm sorry, I meant to go to paragraph (b),
and:
"... as security ... assign its right to
any moneys due or to become due under
the Contract."
On a proper construction, in my
submission, that clause prohibits
an irrevocable assignment after which the
assignee walks away; or alternatively, it
prohibits an assignment of the benefits of the
contract.  It does not apply in any event to
a contractor-controlled subcontract agreement
such as that envisaged by the cooperation
agreement.
What is also said is that there is
a breach of page 9 of that document, which is
1.14; I think it's at the bottom.  I think
I have a bad reference.  Could I have 1.14,
please.  And this applies in the situation of
"a joint venture, [a] consortium or [an]other
unincorporated grouping of two or more
persons".
It's clear, in my submission, that
6th Bureau was a subordinate subcontractor.
It is not a joint adventurer, it is not
a consortium partner.  And this, we say, is
important because it's an example of the
respondent's view of its rights against the
claimant, an example of the respondent's view
going beyond the terms that the parties in fact
agreed, and we say that you will see this again
and again.
As to the law, can I have, please,
{B17-15}, which should be in the respondent's
opening statement.  At 37.1, you will see,
sirs, that the respondent still relies
throughout its opening on the 2020 version of
the Government Contracts Law.
It is wrong to do that.  It has agreed not
to do that, for all of the reasons that I've
addressed you on in great detail.  The fact
that it still does it nonetheless is another
example, we say, of the respondent's attempt to
retrospectively unpack matters that have
already been closed, such as the milestone A
taking-over certificate, such as the deductions
made at the end of the clause 11 process.
And it's mirrored, in my submission, by
the respondent's rejection of its own
engineer's view of the quality and the
completeness of the work that we produced at
the time.  That, like this, is unjustified and
unreasonable.
In any event, the respondent's case theory
on 6th Bureau goes nowhere, we say.  The
reliance on the involvement of 6th Bureau is
said to have the following effect.  Can
I please have {B17-16}.  And if we look at
paragraph 38.2, we see that the point taken
there is, in the last sentence:
"These are losses suffered by 6th Bureau
(not [China State]) and [China State] cannot
quantify its damages claim by reference to
a third party's losses."
The other consequence is in the same
document, please, at page 58, 168.3.  And what
is said:
"There is no evidence ... that
[China State] ever paid 6th Bureau in respect
of [those] costs."
That's the case on which the respondent
has opened as to the consequences of the
6th Bureau involvement; that's the case that
I have come ready to reply to.  And our reply
is this: there is evidence that the costs
claimed by China State in relation to
6th Bureau were paid by China State to
6th Bureau.
So that, we say, is the end of the first
point with which the respondent wished to
introduce its defence and its counterclaim to
you.
The second point relates to notices, and
I think I need to go back for that to page 4 of
the same document, please.  Page 4, sorry, and
I think I've got paragraph 6 in mind.
What is said is that the claimant's claims
were not presented in accordance with
the contract during the life of the project,
therefore there is no entitlement.  There are
three categories, (a), (b), (c), that are
particularly impugned.  The first relates to
delay events.
I'm sorry, before (a):
"These claims principally arise from
delays to the completion of the Works ..."
As to that, I don't think complaint is
necessarily made in toto.  What is said appears
later.  What is said is that even if the
claimant gave notices in relation to the
defects that are identified by Mr Widdowson now
but which were not the subject of an EOT claim
contemporaneously, that makes the claim that
I put before you a completely new claim in
relation to which no notice has been given,
which means that that is a reason for the time
claim to fall in toto.
That, in my submission, just doesn't find
any foundation in sub-clause 20.1.  20.1, as
you know -- to the point I suspect I don't have
to take you there -- requires notice of events
or circumstances.  So the position that's put,
just for your reference, in paragraph 127.1 by
the respondent again goes nowhere.  The
particularisation provisions of 20.1 are not
conditions precedent.
You see at 6(a) the first point of
challenge upon the notices is in relation to
deductions made by DSOA in relation to the
media facade.
Again, sub-clause 20.1, as we all know,
applies where the claimant considers itself to
be entitled to any additional payments under
the contract.  My media facade claim is not
a claim for additional payments under the
contracts; it is a claim to retain the sums
that have already been paid by way of the
original contract price under the contract
which have since been clawed back.  It does not
require any notice under 20.1.
6(b) is finance charges.  The vast
majority of my finance charge claims -- I think
it's something like 30 million out of 32 -- are
parasitic on our response to the respondent's
defects claim.  Again, we do not need notices
in that regard.
We say if that is the basis on which
the -- it's the core and the heart of my
learned friend's claim, we will ask you to
reject it, and we will ask you to conclude
that, on analysis, the matters that they rely
on in fact support our position.
Again, I'm going to step through my
learned friend's opening in the order that he's
taken it, and he starts with delay and with
milestone A completion.  Once again, we say
that the respondent's case on the completion or
otherwise, or the binding nature or otherwise
of the taking-over certificate that has already
been issued in relation to milestone A, is
arid.
The respondent's case is to be found at
page 27 of that document, paragraphs 77 and
77.1.  And I think ... I'm so sorry, I have
a bad reference.  Can I go back a page to
paragraph 75.
What is said is that:
"... [China State]'s failure to complete
Milestone A by 30 June 2019 was a significant
contributory factor to its failure to complete
Milestone B by [the Milestone B completion
date]."
But the delay experts do not highlight any
particular relevance of milestone A or the
milestone exclusion works as causing critical
delay, and Mr Widdowson has analysed the
exclusion works and concluded that they are not
of a nature or of a magnitude that would have
caused delay.
The respondent's case is also that the
milestone A taking-over certificate is not
an admission by it.  As to this, it's important
to note that the milestone A taking-over
certificate is not an engineer's taking-over
certificate.  There are two points there: one
is factual and one is contractual.
You will see in the correspondence -- and
I think we've highlighted this in our written
opening -- that the engineer signed and stamped
and circulated to the project team three drafts
of the taking-over certificate for milestone B.
None of them were approved by the respondent,
therefore none of them were issued.  Therefore
the milestone A taking-over certificate was not
just deemed in contract to be issued as
an action of the respondent, but was in fact
approved by it, signed by it and stamped by it.
Now, that is, in our submission,
an admission.  It is an admission that is
binding on the respondent and is one upon which
it cannot go back.
As to the effect of the milestone A
taking-over certificate, it is, we say, good
evidence that the milestone A works were in
fact practically complete on 30 June 2019.
Why does that matter to you?  It matters
to you because it means that the physical
works, which are milestone A, could not
therefore prevent the achievement of
milestone B on 31 December.  Any physical works
that required completion or correction --
because there were some -- they were snagging
or they were incomplete works that could be
completed within the DLP, pursuant to
clause 10.1 of the general conditions.
So we say that the question for you on
completion of milestone B is: what, if any,
testing and commissioning works, milestone B
works, remained to be complete for the purposes
of supplemental agreement 2 on
31 December 2019?
That brings us to the completion
requirements of supplemental agreement no. 2.
If I may start with the respondent's case
in practical terms.  Could I please have
{C7-44}, which should be Mr Al-Mufti's second
witness statement, and it's paragraph 120 that
I'm interested in.  (Pause)
Paragraph 120.  Again, this is, in
practical terms, what it is that the respondent
says the effect of supplemental agreement no. 2
is.  In the second sentence of paragraph 120:
"There is no distinction in [Supplemental
Agreement] No.2 between 'major' and 'minor'
[testing and commissioning] works for the
purpose of Milestone B completion."
And in the last sentence:
